title: The exact same word can mean three different things — by pitch alone
example_native: 橋 (はし) / 箸 (はし) / 端 (はし)
example_gloss: bridge / chopsticks / edge — all pronounced "hashi," distinguished only by which syllable is pitched higher
bridge_note: There's no spelling or stress difference like English has ("record" the noun vs. "record" the verb) — the entire distinction lives in pitch, something most learners don't even hear at first.

title: You can't just count things — you need the right counting word for their shape
example_native: 一本 (いっぽん) / 一枚 (いちまい) / 一匹 (いっぴき)
example_gloss: one [long thin thing] / one [flat thing] / one [small animal] — three completely different words all meaning "one," chosen by the shape/category of what's being counted
bridge_note: English has a few of these ("a school of fish," "a herd of cattle") but only for specific nouns. Japanese requires picking the right counter for nearly everything you count, every time.

title: A word for sunlight filtering through leaves
example_gloss: literally "tree-leaking sun" — sunlight filtering down through the leaves of trees
bridge_note: It's not "sunlight" and not "shade" — it's specifically the dappled effect of both together, common enough in everyday Japanese to have earned its own word.

title: Politeness can swap out the verb entirely, not just the tone
example_native: 食べる → 召し上がる / いただく
example_gloss: to eat → to eat (respectfully, about someone else) / to eat (humbly, about yourself) — three unrelated-looking verbs for the same action
bridge_note: English adjusts tone and word choice for politeness ("eat" vs. "dine"), but keigo goes further: an entirely different verb depending on whether you're elevating the other person or lowering yourself.

title: Nouns usually don't mark whether there's one or many
example_gloss: cat, or cats — identical either way, with number left entirely to context
bridge_note: English never lets you leave this ambiguous (cat/cats is mandatory). Japanese treats it as something you only bother specifying if it actually matters for what you're saying.

title: A huge class of sound/mood words used in completely ordinary speech
example_native: きらきら / わくわく
example_gloss: sparkling, twinkling / the feeling of excited anticipation
bridge_note: English onomatopoeia is mostly for literal sounds (boom, buzz) and feels a bit childish in adult speech. Japanese mimetic words extend to describing moods, textures, and manners — and are used constantly, at every age, in ordinary conversation.
